en: Leaving not a single one behind;
Every choice swift horse in the valley
Karagul drove into confusion.
Along the separated foothill road
Karagul went,
Cutting the thoroughbreds from the herd,
Karagul drove them on.
Karagul separated the stallions
And took them from the herd;
Karagul had performed
A merciless deed of daring.
Within that herd,
Mares were left without stallions,
And yearlings were left without their sires.
He settled the coursers
On the slopes of Kyr-Kayyn,
At the edge of Suuk-Tör,
And drove the horses away separately.
Taking them where they could not be seen,
To a spur of the distant mountain,
Into the hollow of Kyr-Kayyn,
Karagul brought and left them,
Then halted in that place.
“I had forty horse herders;
He burst in and destroyed them!” he said,
Lamenting what had happened before.
“Semetey, son of the Bloodthirsty One,
If I do not dig your deep grave,
If I do not make your misery boil,
If I do not club you in the water
And show some marvel
To the orphan son of Sultan Manas,
I will take with my sword
The head of that bastard champion,
Drag him from the water,
And make him fit for the Danggits.
I will cut off his head, tie it securely,
And go to hero Kongurbai
To claim the glad tidings.
If I do not perform such a feat,
May I sink away as though never born;
May I die rather than live!”
Saying this, he worked himself up,
Turned wrathful and transformed,
Girded on a sword without a sheath,
And like a cloud about to rain again,
His face turned wrathful.
He sped down into the valley
And raced along the water.
Let us leave him this way
And begin the tale of the rash Semetey,
Who was being swept down the river.
When he had emerged from the water before,
His strength was spent and his breath gone;
When he opened his mouth to say “Ah,”
Water poured out by the wineskin-full.
His power was exhausted and his strength gone,
And the beast like Arbuurul had gone from beneath him.
Deceived by Karagul,
The rash youth had been left in this state.
At the mound by the circling water,
He halted at the mound.
When he had gathered his senses,
He cried out like his mother
And lamented Taibuurul:
“Ah, this accursed, treacherous world!
Will I die in the water?
Will I, this wretched bastard, remain bereft—
Will I ever see Taibuurul?!
Ah, my beloved Taibuurul,
Joined with me when I was no bigger than a louse,
United with me when I was no bigger than a thumb,
Met when I was no bigger than a tick,
My thoroughbred ridden into battle!
Külchoro and Kanchoro
Are my two brothers from the same nest;
They joined what had been severed
And gathered what had been scattered.
Alas, my kinsman Bakai, in this woeful hour!
There is no thoroughbred like Taibuurul
For me to catch and ride here;
There is no kinsman Külchoro or Bakai
To come to my aid.
One seen today is gone tomorrow—
Is this what you are, filthy world!
There is no forest into which I can flee,
And no Kyrgyz to come to my aid.
I would not be deceived by a deceiver—
Can my strength have fallen this far?
Or have I no waist left to gird,
No renowned companion and lion
Upon whom I relied?
I must have come to behold
This vast, impassable river;
Deceived by the frenzied slave,
I must have come here to die.
Rather than remain alive in the world,
What did I mean to do?
I must have meant to depart
This world all the sooner!
Will there be a day when I wear
Akolpok, left by my father Manas?
Will there be a day when I mount
The ever-ready Buurul?
Will there be a day when I drive
The frenzied slave toward Beijing?
The one who leapt far beyond the chasm,
Whom I guarded more dearly than my father Manas—
May he never age, may Taibuurul never age!”
Speaking thus, Semetey,
With life barely remaining,
Felt anguish smoke fiercely within him;
He lost his strength in grief,
And black night descended upon him.
Red-roan, with a low mane,
The ever-ready Arbuurul
Had come beside him.
He had no tongue with which to speak,
Yet the creature was wiser than a man.
When he heard Semetey’s voice,
Buurul came out from among the horses;
Within the herd, that thoroughbred
Had heard Semetey’s voice.
Neighing and snorting,
Pounding the black earth,
Tossing his forelock toward the sky,
Driving his hooves into the ground,
Drawing in his belly as he neighed,
Taibuurul stood there.
Arching his neck like a duck,
Arbuurul bent down.
The horse Buurul knew
That Semetey was in the water.
When he saw Semetey,
As though seeing his own foal,
Into the flowing river,
Neighing six or seven times,
Buurul the horse entered.
Great Buurul, bobbing his head,
Now reached
Hero Semetey.
He held out his great tail,
Thick as an armful.
“Buurul has come to me;
This is the place where I will not die,” he thought,
And the orphan’s eyes lit up.
In that woeful hour he grasped
The great tail
Of the prancing, ever-ready Buurul.
Once his lord had taken hold of the tail,
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
Buurul began to drag him.
The great lord did not die from his rashness,
But emerged from the water—
The great lord emerged
From the vast, impassable torrent.
The hero had lost consciousness,
The heedless-born lion,
A hero born after
His father Manas, the gray wolf,
And left by his noble father Manas
The Akolpok he had inherited.
Its collar was gold and its sleeves copper,
With paired mail-rings and lark-eye links,
A keleме coat of broad mail,
Impenetrable by bullets when worn in battle.
Its lining was worked in silk;
The formidable Lady Kanykei
Had bitten and worked it for twelve years.
She strengthened its weave exceedingly
And made bullets glance aside from it.
Enemies who came out shooting
Collapsed when they found no way through.
While making Akolpok,
She depleted a great part
Of his father’s treasury.
Through her toil, Kanykei
Gave Akolpok as a gift:
“My only son will wear it;
He will attack the enemy without tiring.
He will say, ‘My mother was incomparable,’
And understand my worth.”
Unable to gather his senses and put on
His mother’s Akolpok,
The hunched, rash hero
Could not mount Arbuurul.
At times his mind wandered;
A red haze appeared
Before the poor youth’s clouded eyes.
His gaze wandered distractedly,
And his entire body
Hung utterly slack and would not gather itself.
The splendid hero, son of Manas,
Stood unable to catch his breath.
Rushing forward upon Algara,
God had struck the slave.
When he saw Semetey,
Karagul worked himself into a frenzy,
Thundered in fury,
And addressed Semetey:
“Kürpüldök, from bank to bank—
This is the road I myself reconnoitered;
This is the host that deceived
Your rash father Manas six times.
Know this, gray wolf Karagul:
You have come to behold it;
You have come from the Kakan
To die, without remaining alive.
I am the valiant man who drew bows
Like pouring rain against
Your rash father Manas;
I am the valiant man who inflicted
Humiliation no person had ever seen!
You have come to behold
The wrath of Karagul.
Great rash son of the Bloodthirsty One,
You have come here to die!”
Saying this, Karagul
Now gathered his courage.
A forty-fathom lasso with a black strap,
A catch-rope made of birch—
He spat upon his hand and grasped it,
Held the narrow end and swung it,
And with its thick end struck the hero,
Sending it crashing against his crown.
What else could a slave devour?
Semetey stood grieving;
A full span of scalp
Had been torn away.
Then Semetey—
Have you heard of him?—
Offspring of the blood-drinker,
Offspring of the accursed one
Who set fire to grassy land,
Manas the leopard’s own son,
Who poured blood into black water,
Who set the tussocked land ablaze,
Who cut off a head when told, “Take his cap,”
Who spilled a life when told, “Spill blood,”
Who seized the grief-stricken—
When his wrath was roused,
He killed his own father.
Hot blood reached his nostrils;
From his neck and jaw
Blood streamed like a saddle-strap.
He flared higher whenever diminished,
And multiplied whenever slain—
The accursed one’s own son.
When the lasso struck his head,
He shouted in fury,
Invoking the name of Manas,
Who had gone to the other world:
“Frenzied slave, is it you?
May I die if my strength does not suffice!
Wrathful Karagul,
